claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by rapid formation of a chromium-enriched passive film.
Chromium is selectively oxidized preferentially at grain boundaries.
A high grain-boundary density accelerates chromium diffusion from the bulk to the surface.
Formation of the chromium-enriched film reduces local galvanic coupling.
Reduced local galvanic coupling limits corrosion.
Severe plastic deformation can produce an ultrafine-grained bulk steel microstructure.
An ultrafine-grained structure has a higher grain-boundary density than the coarse-grained baseline.
Conventional steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power equipment have baseline levels of chromium, nickel, and molybdenum.
Acidic or chloride-containing aqueous solutions at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures represent typical chemical-processing corrosion environments.
High-temperature, high-pressure water or molten salts represent nuclear-power corrosion environments.
The enhanced grain-boundary network causes faster formation of a uniform chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
The resulting chromium-enriched passive film is continuous and protective against further corrosive attack.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steels generally show improved corrosion resistance relative to coarse-grained stainless steels.
The refined steel will have a lower corrosion current density than the coarse-grained control.
The refined steel will form a thicker passive film than the coarse-grained control.
The refined steel will form a more uniform and more chromium-rich passive film than the coarse-grained control.
The proposed mechanism should hold provided that excessive mechanical or thermal shocks do not disrupt passive-film integrity.
Other alloying elements and environmental conditions can influence the corrosion response.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can experimentally assess chromium enrichment in the passivation film.
Failure of the refined steel to show either lower corrosion current density or a more enriched and uniform chromium-rich film would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis extends the chromium-passivation mechanism to molten-salt nuclear environments, but the cited molten-salt evidence states that chromium is typically the alloying element most vulnerable to fluoride-salt corrosion. This makes the proposed molten-salt boundary insufficiently qualified.
